articles.title: From ad to application

body.support:
A job **application** is more than a resume. It is a kit.

**1. Decode the ad.** Find:
- the job and the employer.
- what they **must** have.
- what would be nice to have.
- how to apply, and by when.

**2. Tailor your resume.** **Tailor** means make it fit this job.
- Put the most useful things first.
- Use the same words as the ad.
- Give proof. “Never late in 18 months.”.

**3. Write a cover email.**
- A clear subject line.
- Say which job.
- Say two reasons you fit.
- Say thanks. Sign off with your name and phone number.
.
**4. Be ready to talk.** They might call. Have a short **pitch** ready: who you are, what you can do, why you want this job.

**5. Check it all.** Spelling. Phone number. Email address. Does it all match?
body.core:
A job application is a **kit** of texts that work together. Each has a different job.

**1. Decode the ad.** Every ad tells you what the employer wants, if you read it carefully.
- **Essential criteria:** what you must have (a licence, a White Card, weekend availability).
- **Desirable criteria:** what would help.
- **Their key words:** “reliable”, “customer focus”, “team player”.
- **How to apply** and the closing date.

**2. Tailor your resume.** One page is usually enough for a first job. **Tailor** it for each ad:
- put your most relevant experience first (paid work, volunteering, sport, school roles all count).
- use the ad’s key words where they’re true for you.
- give proof: numbers, results and responsibilities.
- list skills and tickets that match the criteria.
- include two **referees** (ask them first).

**3. Write a cover email.** This is a formal email. It’s often the first thing an employer reads.
- **Subject:** Application: Apprentice Carpenter, [your name].
- **Greeting:** Dear [name], or Dear Hiring Manager.
- **Paragraph 1:** the job, and where you saw it.
- **Paragraph 2:** two or three reasons you fit, with proof.
- **Paragraph 3:** when you’re available, and thanks.
- **Sign-off:** Kind regards, full name, phone.
- Attach your resume as a PDF.

**4. Prepare your pitch.** If they call, you need a 30-second answer to “Tell me about yourself”: who you are, what you can offer, why this job.

**5. Make it consistent.** Your resume, email and pitch should tell the same story about you.
body.extend:
A job application is a set of linked texts, each with its own conventions and audience: busy employers screening many applicants.

**1. Analyse the ad.** Identify **essential** and **desirable criteria**, key words that signal the employer’s values, and practical details (hours, location, closing date, how to apply). Note the tone: corporate, casual, community-focused.

**2. Tailor the resume.** A first resume is usually one page. Tailor it to each ad:
- order sections by relevance; for many young applicants, skills and experience matter more than school details.
- frame paid work, volunteering, sport and school roles as evidence against the criteria.
- use action verbs and specific results.
- mirror the ad’s key words honestly.
- include licences, tickets and referees (with permission).

**3. Write the cover email.** A formal email shows your written communication and your fit:
- a precise subject line naming the role and you.
- an opening that names the role and source.
- a body with two or three criterion-matched claims, each with evidence.
- a close covering availability and appreciation.
- professional sign-off and contact details; resume attached as a PDF.

**4. Prepare the spoken pitch.** Phone screens and interviews often open with “Tell me about yourself”. An **elevator pitch** of about 30 seconds covers who you are, what you offer and why this role. Deliver it with a steady pace, warmth and confidence.

**5. Consistency.** Each text should reinforce one message about you, so the employer sees the same candidate on paper and on the phone.

caseStudies.title: What employers check first

body.support:
A government group asks bosses how they choose new workers. It is called **Jobs and Skills Australia**.

In **2024**, it wrote a report. It is called **How employers recruit**.

About **half** of bosses check one thing first. Does the person show they have done this kind of work? Do they have the right skills?

Bosses also want the right **personal qualities**. Things like being on time and keen to learn.

So your kit needs to show both. Show what you can do. Show what you are like.
body.core:
**Jobs and Skills Australia** is a government agency. It asks employers how they hire.

In **July 2024**, it put out a report called **How employers recruit**. When employers first look at applications, about **half** check one thing. Does the person show **relevant experience and skills**?

Across many kinds of jobs, employers mostly wanted two things. They wanted **relevant work experience**. They also wanted the right **personal qualities**, like being reliable, keen and good with people.

That’s hard if you haven’t had many jobs. But “experience” can include volunteering, sport, school roles and casual work. You just need to show how they match what the employer wants.

A tailored application does exactly that.
body.extend:
**Jobs and Skills Australia** runs a regular survey that asks employers how they hire.

Its **July 2024** report, **How employers recruit**, found that about **half** of employers check one thing first. Does the applicant show **relevant experience and skills**? Across job types, employers mostly wanted **relevant work experience**, plus the right set of **personal qualities**.

Another 2024 report found that a lack of experience was one of the main reasons employers struggled to fill jobs.

For young applicants, this is a familiar trap: you need experience to get experience. The research points to a practical way out. Employers look for *evidence* of relevant experience and qualities. So your task is to turn what you have done into evidence that matches the criteria. That could be casual work, volunteering, sport, school leadership or VM work placements.

A tailored application is not just polite. It’s how you get past the first check.

teacher.overview: A VM 3&4 capstone. Students build a complete, consistent application kit for a real job, apprenticeship, placement or volunteer role: a decoded ad, a matched evidence table, a tailored resume, a formal cover email and a 30-second spoken pitch, tested in a mock call. The case study is Jobs and Skills Australia’s July 2024 report “How employers recruit”: about half of employers check at the application stage whether applicants show relevant experience and skills, and employers mostly want relevant experience plus suitable personal attributes.
prep: Collect real local job ads (SEEK, Indeed, shop windows, apprenticeship networks), or ask students to bring one.
Devices for typing the final resume and email.
Arrange mock callers (staff, careers adviser, family).
Students should have done some of On the Job and Advocate first (this capstone requires two from each).

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Decode and match
steps: **Hook (5 min):** what would make you skip an application if you were the boss?
**Steps 1–2 (20 min):** decode the ad and match.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Case and resume
steps: **Case study (15 min):** what employers check first.
**Sort (10 min):** send it or fix it.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Pitch
steps: **Do it (35 min):** write, rehearse and do mock calls.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 — Finish
steps: **Final polish (30 min):** save PDF, final check.

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 subject naming job and applicant; 2 formal greeting; 3 purpose and source; 4 the employer’s key word plus proof; 5 availability; 6 sign-off with phone and attachment.

**Sort:** send — clear subject line; tickets list; referees who were asked. Fix — “hey, saw ur ad” (too casual); silly email address; “I just need money” (say why this job).

**Case study:** about half of employers check at the application stage whether applicants show relevant experience and skills; employers mostly want relevant experience plus suitable personal attributes; young people can translate volunteering, sport, school roles and casual work into matched evidence.

realityCheck: **Real ads make it real.** If students actually send their kit, celebrate it, and help them follow up.
**Students with no paid work** often undervalue sport, caring roles, volunteering and VM placements. The match table is where you help them see it.
**Referees must be asked first.** Make that a checkpoint.
**Privacy:** remind students not to put their home address or date of birth on a resume.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Mock calls with unfamiliar adults are nerve-racking but hugely valuable.
